question.text: Given that \[ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \] express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2+3x_1x_2 + x_2^2$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that

\[ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \]

gives the following expressions for $y_1$ and $y_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} y_1 &= x_1+2x_2 \\[3pt] y_2 &= -x_2 \end{align*}

By solving the second equation for $x_2$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} x_1 &= y_1+2y_2 \\[3pt] x_2 &= -y_2 \end{align*}

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

\begin{align*} Q(\mathbf{x}) &= x_1^2+3x_1x_2 + x_2^2 \\[3pt] &= (y_1+2y_2)^2+3(y_1+2y_2)(-y_2) + (-y_2)^2 \\[3pt] &= y_1^2+4y_1y_2+4y_2^2 - 3y_1y_2 - 6y_2^2 + y_2^2 \\[3pt] &= y_1^2 + y_1y_2-y_2^2 \end{align*}

question.text: Given that \[ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \] express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2+5x_1x_2 - x_2^2$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that

\[ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \]

gives the following expressions for $y_1$ and $y_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} y_1 &= x_1 \\[3pt] y_2 &= -x_1-x_2 \end{align*}

By solving the first equation for $x_1$ and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} x_1 &= y_1 \\[3pt] x_2 &=-y_1 -y_2 \end{align*}

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

\begin{align*} Q(\mathbf{x}) &= x_1^2+5x_1x_2 - x_2^2 \\[3pt] &= y_1^2+5y_1(-y_1-y_2) - (-y_1-y_2)^2 \\[3pt] &= y_1^2-5y_1^2-5y_1y_2-y_1^2 - 2y_1y_2 - y_2^2 \\[3pt] &= -5y_1^2 -7 y_1y_2-y_2^2 \end{align*}

question.text: Given that \[ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \] express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2+x_1x_2-2x_2^2 $ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that

\[ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \]

gives the following expressions for $y_1$ and $y_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} y_1 &= x_2 \\[3pt] y_2 &= -x_1 \end{align*}

Solving these for $x_1$ and $x_2$, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} x_1 &=-y_2 \\[3pt] x_2 &= y_1 \end{align*}

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

\begin{align*} Q(\mathbf{x}) &= x_1^2+x_1x_2-2x_2^2\\[3pt] &= (-y_2)^2+(-y_2)y_1-2y_1^2 \\[3pt] &= y_2^2- y_2y_1 -2y_1^2 \\[3pt] &=-2 y_1^2 - y_1 y_2 +y_2^2 \end{align*}

example.title: Changing Variables in a Quadratic Form Given New Variables Through Old Variables

question.text: \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $\mathbf{x}=[x_1, x_2]^T$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $\mathbf{y}=[ y_1, y_2 ]^T$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then

\[ \mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}. \]

As a result, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} &= (P\mathbf{y})^T \! A \, (P\mathbf{y}) \\[3pt] &= (\mathbf{y}^TP^T) \, A \, (P\mathbf{y}) \\[3pt] &= \mathbf{y}^T(P^T \! A P) \, \mathbf{y}, \end{align*}

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

\begin{align*} P^T \! A P &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 5 \\ 5 & 11 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

question.text: \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $\mathbf{x}=[x_1, x_2]^T$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $\mathbf{y}=[ y_1, y_2 ]^T$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then

\[ \mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}. \]

As a result, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} &= (P\mathbf{y})^T \! A \, (P\mathbf{y}) \\[3pt] &= (\mathbf{y}^TP^T) \, A \, (P\mathbf{y}) \\[3pt] &= \mathbf{y}^T(P^T \! A P) \, \mathbf{y}, \end{align*}

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

\begin{align*} P^T \! A P &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &9 \\ 5 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 9 \\ 9 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
